headline: Deer Island's Outgoing Water Still Holds Bass — But I'm Running North This Week
subhead: Harbor bass are sliding deeper as August warms the flats, and the bluefish under the bunker pods are exactly where we said they'd be.
body_markdown:
Every Thursday this time of year I make the same call at the chart table: harbor, rocks, or run south to Plymouth. This week I'm splitting the difference — working the harbor early before the sun gets up on the flats, then pushing out to the Nahant side for the evening tide. Here's why.

Boston Harbor in the first week of August is a warm-water harbor, and warm water pushes bass off the shallow flats and onto structure where there's moving water and shade. Deer Island's outer edge, where the flow rips past on the outgoing tide, is still holding fish — but they're not sitting up shallow anymore. They've dropped into the deeper cuts along the drop-off, tucked against the rockpile where the current breaks. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or a chunk of fresh bunker fished on the bottom with just enough weight to hold in the current, has been the more consistent producer than plugs up top during the brightest hours. Once the tide starts to soften on the last of the ebb, that's when the topwater window opens — poppers and Danny-style swimmers worked along the current seam near Spectacle Island have drawn bass up out of the depth, especially if there's bunker in the area.

And there has been bunker. We flagged this pattern two weeks back — that as long as high pressure held and bunker schools stayed thick, the bluefish would keep punishing them on top — and that's exactly the shape of things right now. Wherever those pods concentrate around the harbor islands and along the Winthrop side, the blues are underneath them, and it's violent, visible feeding: birds working, bait skying, blues cutting through like a lawnmower. A wire leader ahead of a single-hook popper or a Hopkins spoon worked fast through the melee will draw strikes almost every cast when the blitz is on. The catch is timing — these pods move, and they don't sit still for long. If you find the birds, don't waste time getting the boat into position; that window can close in ten minutes.

Flounder, I'll be honest, are a tough sell in early August. The harbor's flounder bite is a spring and fall program — cooler water, less current stress on the fish. Right now they're scattered and lethargic on the muddy bottoms inside the harbor, and if you're targeting them specifically, expect a slow pick rather than a program. I wouldn't build a trip around them this week.

North Shore rock structure is where I think the better light-tackle program is right now. From Nahant up through the Cape Ann shoreline, the bass have settled into their August pattern — holding tight to the ledges and boulder fields, feeding hardest on the edges of light, meaning first light and last light, with a secondary window around the turn of the tide when baitfish get pushed off the rocks. Eels fished at night along the base of those ledges remain the most dependable bass producer on this stretch, and if you're not an eel angler, a soft plastic like a jointed swimbait or a rigged rubber shad, worked slow and just off bottom, will cover the same water without live bait logistics. The rocky spine running out toward Gloucester holds fish in the same way it has for generations — current, cover, and depth close together. That's the formula. Find where those three things overlap and you've found the fish.

Mackerel have thinned out compared to where they were a month ago, which tracks with the seasonal pattern — by August they've largely pushed farther offshore and north, leaving the inshore jigging bite spottier than it was in June. If you're counting on filling a livewell with mackerel for bait, budget extra time; it's not the reliable five-minute program it was earlier in the summer.

South toward Plymouth, Duxbury Bay, and Kingston Bay, the water tends to run a touch warmer and the structure is softer — sand and eelgrass rather than granite — so the bass program down there leans more on moving bait and current edges than hard structure. It's a legitimate option if the North Shore rocks get crowded or the wind swings onshore and makes fishing the ledges uncomfortable, but I'd call it the backup plan this week, not the primary target.

Cod and haddock remain a cold-water, deeper-structure story, and this time of year that fishery is thin close to shore — the better grounds are farther out past where most of this beat's light-tackle program operates, and what's available inshore right now is inconsistent enough that I wouldn't plan a trip around it until the water starts cooling again in the fall.

Looking ahead, if the bunker stay thick and the high pressure holds through the week, I'd expect the bluefish blitzes to keep showing up on the harbor's edges, and the bass to hold their pattern on structure until there's a real cooling event or a wind shift stirs things up. If a front does come through and drops the surface temps even a couple of degrees, watch for bass to push back up shallower and feed harder during the day — that's the signal to shift the game plan back toward the flats and away from the deep ledges.
